(AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura) Hundreds of thousands of people were left without power after storms hit the East and West coasts, prompting road closures and flight delays on Thanksgiving. Around 700,000 homes remain without power as of 3 a.m. ET Friday, on the East coast and in areas of Missouri. Weather warnings are in place along the East and West coasts for gales and hazardous seas, respectively, while a handful of states in the Northeast and Northwest of the country are under winter weather advisories. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Thanksgiving saw thousands of flight delays and hundreds of cancellations, as well as road flooding in coastal areas and heavy snowfall in areas of Illinois and Missouri. There were more than 2,500 flight delays and 462 cancellations within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware . This follows more than 7,000 delays Wednesday as travelers attempted to make their way across the country to celebrate Thanksgiving. The storm flooded coastal areas along the Eastern Seaboard from North Carolina through New Jersey, with highways and roads shut down due to floodwaters and high winds. More than 830,000 homes and businesses were without power yesterday, led by Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia, according to PowerOutage.us , with more than 100,000 having power restored by early Friday. Advertisement Advertisement About 42 million people were under high wind warnings or wind advisories as of 4:50 a.m. ET, and around 64 million are under coastal flood warnings or advisories, according to the National Weather Service . In New York City, a state of emergency was declared by Gov. Kathy Hochul and the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed until Saturda y. California battled surging king tides with an entire section of the Pacifica Pier demolished by waves. Borough officials said in a Facebook post the flooding was expected to continue throughout Thursday, and they urged everyone to stay off the roads. An estimated 3 to 4 feet of water flooded the area, according to nearby tidal gauges.
